#5385. Genesis AI Raises $500M At $3.5B Valuation To Bring Its Robots To Factories And Warehouses

Genesis AI, a startup teaching robots to perform physical tasks by learning from human movements, announced Tuesday it has raised $500 million in Series A funding at a $3.5 billion valuation.

Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the round, which brings the company’s disclosed funding to $605 million since its 2024 inception. Genesis previously raised $105 million in a round announced in July 2025.

The company is developing both robots and the AI software that controls them. Its approach combines recordings of human hand movements with training in simulated environments, where robots can practice skills before attempting them in the physical world.

Genesis is initially targeting manufacturing, logistics and laboratories with its robot, Eno.

“We just want to bring something more elegant, more timeless,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian told Crunchbase News in an interview. “In the end, this is a very full-stack company. … We have to build all different pieces across the entire stack to make sure we can tightly integrate our technology stack together, and hopefully build the most well-polished and reliable product.

Other participants in the new financing include T. Rowe Price Associates, Durable Capital Partners, Bpifrance, HSG, Nvidia, AMD Ventures, Zoom, Samsung Next and Ericsson. Individual backers include Eric Schmidt, Eric Yuan, Jerry Yang, Xavier Niel and Zach Kirkhorn.

The company plans to use the capital to expand its computing infrastructure, increase robot production and hire more employees, Xian told Crunchbase News. Presently, Genesis has close to 100 employees. It is headquartered in Paris, with offices in San Carlos, California.

Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with most of the investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data.

The closely related field of physical AI has also seen a surge in venture investment this year.

Genesis’s approach grew out of a challenge Xian encountered during his robotics research: The difficulty of finding enough examples for robots to learn from.

Language models have vast amounts of text to draw on. But robots need a different kind of data to learn how to move and for example, pick up and handle objects. They also need that data to better understand what they’re touching and what happens when they act.

Genesis works by using cameras and gloves to capture people’s hand and finger movements as they work, along with touch information. The company says its robotic hand closely matches the human hand and recording glove, making it easier for robots to learn those movements. Historically, collecting this kind of training data involves hiring people to remotely control robots, Xian said. Genesis aims to collect it from people doing their regular jobs instead.

Those recordings help train the company’s AI model, GENE. Genesis also uses its simulation software, Genesis World, to train and test robot skills in virtual environments. The company claims this speeds up a process that would take longer with physical machines alone.

Genesis traces its origins to a research collaboration Xian started in 2022, also named Genesis, while he was pursuing a robotics Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University. The project brought together researchers from more than a dozen universities to develop robotics simulation tools.

After graduating at the end of 2024, Xian teamed up with Theophile Gervet and decided to start a company. Genesis formally launched in March 2025 and expanded beyond simulation into AI software and robot hardware.

Xian said developing those components together would help Genesis make them work reliably as a finished product.

“That requires the intelligence, hardware and everything that goes into training and testing the robots to work as one system,” he said.

Genesis is exploring a rental model in which customers would pay for the robot and its software as a combined service. It has announced a partnership with LG CNS and has other Fortune 500 companies in its prospective customer pipeline, according to Xian. He declined to disclose revenue and did not provide a paying customer count.

Premji Invest partner Vedant Agrawal said in a release that the firm was drawn to demonstrations of robots completing extended tasks independently.

“Completing full tasks in real time, not just short clips, is what turns a robot into something a business can rely on,” he said.

Genesis says it is ramping up Eno production for industrial customers. Looking ahead, it plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare, then consumer and outdoor uses.

#5384. Tech Moves: Microsoft names 2 leaders, loses 1; DoorDash VP departs; BluePill, Glacis get execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 11:47 am

— Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile.

Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”

— Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said.

Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.

He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.”

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform launched in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

— BluePill, a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” said Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

— Glacis, a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

In a post announcing the new role, Sanders said she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

— The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

— Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for the University of Washington AI and Machine Learning for Engineering programs and the UW NSF AI Institute for Dynamic Systems. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/19 to correct that Charlie Trillingham worked for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business, not the Foster School itself.

#5383. October 22, 2019

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed plans for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too quickly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”

Blueground, a six-year-old, New York-based startup providing turnkey flexible rental apartments, has raised $50 million in Series B funding, roughly six months after raising $20 million in Series A funding. WestCap Investment Partners and Prime Ventures co-led the round. More here.

Databricks, a six-year-old, San Francisco-based SaaS business that’s built on top of a bunch of open source tools, has raised a massive $400 million in Series F funding at a post-money valuation of $6.2 billion valuation. Today’s funding brings the total raised to almost a $900 million. Andreessen Horowitz led the round with new investors BlackRock,  T. Rowe Price Associates, and Tiger Global Management also participating. TechCrunch has more here.

IonQ, a four-year-old, College Park, Md.-based startup that uses charged particles suspended in a vacuum, as the basis for its hardware, has raised $55 million in funding. Samsung and Mubadala Capital co-led the round, joined by Amazon, GV, and New Enterprise Associates. Fortune has more here.

Aurora Insight, a three-year-old, Washington, D.C.-based startup that provides a “dynamic” global map of wireless connectivity that it built and monitors in real time using AI combined with data from sensors on satellites, vehicles, buildings, aircraft and other objects, has raised $18 million in Series A funding. Alsop Louie Partners and True Ventures co-led the round,  joined by Tippet Venture Partners, Rise of the Rest Seed Fund, Promus Ventures, Alumni Ventures Group, ValueStream Ventures, and Intellectus Partners. TechCrunch has more here.

Benevity, an 11-year-old, Calgary, Alberta-based company that makes corporate social responsibility and employee engagement software, has raised $30.5 million in Series C funding from General Atlantic and JMI Equity. More here. EV Connect, a 10-year-old, L.A.-based company that sells software to manage electric vehicle charging, has raised $12 million in a Series B round led by Mitsui & Co. and Ecosystem Integrity Fund. The company has raised $25 million to date. TechCrunch has more here.

Octave, a year-old, San Francisco-based tech-based behavioral health practice, has raised $11 million in Series A funding led by Greycroft, with participation from Obvious Ventures and earlier backers. The company has raised at least $14 million to date. Crunchbase News has more here.Signal AI, a six-year-old, London-based business intelligence and media monitoring startup, has raised $25 million in Series C funding. Redline Capital led the round, joined by MMC Ventures, GMG Ventures, and Hearst Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

AllWork, a 3.5-year-old, New York-based on-demand work platform that’s targeting large enterprise customers in need of temporary workers, has raised $3.8 million in seed funding from Great Oaks, Lightspeed Scout Fund, The Fund, Fernbrook, SmartHub, and numerous angel investors. More here.

Beem, a year-old, Boston-based CBD company that’s marketing its branded oils, protein bars, and a salve to athletes who may be looking for alternatives to chemically derived pain relievers and anti-inflammatories, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by Obvious Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

Intrepida Bio, a newly launched, San Diego-based biotech focused on modulating innate immune systems, has raised $9.5 million from Sofinnova and Canaan Partners. FierceBiotech has more here.

LabGenius, a seven-year-old, London-based startup that’s applying AI and robotic automation to protein drug discovery, has raised $10 million in Series A funding. The round was led by Lux Capital and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Felicis Ventures, Inovia Capital, Air Street Capital and earlier investors, along with numerous notable individuals. TechCrunch has more here.

Margin Edge, a four-year-old, Falls Church, Va.-based maker of restaurant management software, has raised $5 million in Series A funding led by Osage Venture Partners, with participation from Good Company. More here.

Medinas, a two-year-old, Berkeley, Ca.-based company that helps healthcare organizations resell their surplus medical equipment and supplies, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by NFX. Additional investors in the round include Precursor Ventures, Sound Ventures, FJ Labs and Bryan Frist (of HCA Healthcare’s founding family). Crunchbase News has more here.

MediView XR, a two-year-old, Cleveland, Oh.-based medical device company working on a surgical navigation system that leverages augmented reality and spatial computing to provide surgeons with advanced visualization, has raised $4.5 million in seed funding. Backers include Inside View Investment,Plug and Play Ventures and Northwest Ohio Tech Fund. More here.

Reibus, a year-old, Atlanta, Ga.-based online marketplace for industrial materials, has raised $3.25 million in seed funding led by Bowery Capital, with participation from Initialized Capital and Stage 2 Capital. More here.

Marcelo Claure, the chief operating officer of SoftBank Group, will assume the position of executive chairman of the board of directors of WeWork when the company receives a planned $1.5 billion payment from SoftBank. TechCrunch has more here.

John Donahoe, the current president and CEO of ServiceNow, is taking over as the CEO and president of Nike in January, replacing Mark Parker who has been since 2006 and lived through numerous controversies over the years. Donahoe knows Nike well, having joined its board, where he will retain a seat, since 2014. In the meantime, Parker will become the company’s executive chairman and Bill McDermott, who abruptly resigned as the longtime CEO of SAP earlier this month for reasons that weren’t clear, is taking over as CEO of ServiceNow. The company’s shareholders apparently prefer Donahoe, who is also the chairman of PayPal and a former CEO of eBay, which he led from 2008 through 2015. At least, shares of ServiceNow dropped in price on the news.

Zaz Floreani has joined the Austin-based venture firm Next Coast Ventures as a principal. Floreani was most recently the VP of corporate development at the same-day delivery company Dropoff. More here.

Manuel Henriquez, founder and former CEO of Hercules Growth Technology Capital, and his wife Elizabeth have both pleaded guilty for their roles in the college admissions cheating scandal. She is to be sentenced Feb. 7 and her husband on March 5. The San Jose Mercury News has more here.

#5382. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5381. Sector Snapshot: Investors Turn Up The Volume On Voice AI

Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work.

Companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology.

The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation.

The funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession.

The numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data shows. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025.

The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents.

The biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI, which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based company is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners.

San Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners, completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital-led financing in April. The company provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models.

Customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV, at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels.

Meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners, at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation.

Among companies focused on AI-generated speech, New York-based ElevenLabs announced a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The company is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing.

Beijing-based ModelBest, which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July.

Voice AI companies have also begun delivering exits. In January, Deepgram acquired OfOne, which automates restaurant and drive-thru orders.

In September, Inworld acquired Ultravox, a developer of conversational voice AI technology.

The sector also saw an IPO. Neosapience, the South Korean company behind synthetic voice platform Typecast, listed on the KOSDAQ on Sept. 21.

Looking ahead, additional acquisitions are in the pipeline. Automation Anywhere agreed to acquire Boost.ai, an enterprise voice and chat AI provider, in October. And Deepgram announced plans to acquire Daily, creator of the Pipecat voice-agent framework.

More recently, Five9 agreed to acquire Level AI for $325 million in cash, adding technology that analyzes customer conversations, assists contact-center workers and automates voice and digital interactions. The Level AI transaction is expected to close by year’s end.

Overall, the space is booming, and it doesn’t look like interest in voice AI will die anytime soon. Tom Hulme, managing partner and head of Europe at GV, told Crunchbase News in 2025 that one of the most exciting trends he believes is underway in the growth of voice AI is that “we’re returning to humanity’s most natural form of communication.”

After decades of adapting ourselves to technology, “technology is finally adapting to us,” he said.

#5380. October 23, 2019

That WeWork deal could fall apart yet, suggests a new Bloomberg report that states SoftBank Group will seek approval of its bailout package with the Committee on Foreign Investment in the U.S., which has stymied SoftBank before. As the report notes: “SoftBank won approval from the panel to buy Sprint Corp. and U.K. chip designer ARM Holdings. However, the committee put conditions on its ownership of Sprint, and restricted its control of alternative-asset manager Fortress Investment Group. More recently, SoftBank was unable to fill two board seats at one of its portfolio companies, Uber Technologies, because it did not have Cfius approval.”

Tesla delivered a strong third-quarter earnings report after the bell today, posting a surprise profit and telling shareholders it’s ahead of schedule with a new factory in Shanghai. Shares rose more than 20 percent after hours. CNBC has more here.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing company was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.)

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the company’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”

Fabric, a four-year-old, New York-based startup that wants to make automated logistics available to retailers of all sizes, has raised $110 million in Series B funding. Corner Ventures led the round, joined by Aleph, CPPIB, Innovation Endeavors, La Maison, Playground Ventures, and Temasek. TechCrunch has more here.

Disperse, a four-year-old, London-based startup whose computer vision-driven construction software aims to identify issues on a site, has raised $15 million in Series A funding led by Northzone. VentureBeat has more here.

Fairmarkit, a two-year-old, Boston-based procurement platform that tries to find the best vendors for its enterprise customers, has raised $11 million in Series A funding led by Insight Partners. Built in Boston has more here.

Lemon Way, a 12-year-old, Paris-based payment processor for marketplaces and crowdfunding platforms, has raised €25 million from Toscafund Asset Management. Tech.eu has more here.

Literati, a three-year-old, Austin, Tex.-based subscription book service for kids, has raised $12 million in funding led by Shasta Ventures. Crunchbase News has more here.

PeerNova, a six-year-old, San Jose, Ca.-based company that aims to enables financial institutions to perpetually synchronize their data across multiple internal and external systems, has raised $31 million in funding. Mosaik Partners led the round, and was joined by Medici Ventures and Intuitive Venture Partners. #5379. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5378. What To Measure When ARR Isn’t Enough

In October, reports that OpenAI‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business?

The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it showed how much weight public markets now place on a single private company’s numbers.

For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing.

ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting.

The first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month.

What gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts.

Companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable.

Take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter.

These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that.

If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size.

Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises.

Retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked.

ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon.

What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could.

Kenza Zayani is an early-stage investor at RTP Global, based in London. She is drawn to ambitious founders tackling the most challenging problems, with a particular interest in AI from infrastructure to applications. Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to company building with founders.

#5376. Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#5375. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

#5374. October 25, 2019

And it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.]

Before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”

Note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity plans, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a new book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

It’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his company, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz says creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this new book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

It’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

You’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

[Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that says [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

As with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Right, everybody knew how Travis was running the company. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

Travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

And he was making everybody so much money. And the company was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’

To me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.

Tonkean, a 4.5-year-old, San Francisco-based robotic automation and management platform for workflows, has raised $7.2 million in seed funding led by Foundation Capital, with participation from Magma Venture Partners and Slow Ventures. More here.

Sequoia Capital founder Don Valentine passed way at his home in Woodside, Ca., today at age 87 of natural causes. Sequoia posted a tribute to Valentine shortly afterward, calling him “one of a generation of leaders who forged Silicon Valley.”  A native of New York, Valentine majored in chemistry at Fordham University before joining Raytheon in South California, then moving north to the Bay Area to work at Fairchild Semiconductor, where over the years, Valentine began investing his own small checks into technology companies that he was meeting. According to Sequoia Capital, he soon attracted the attention of an early mutual fund group, Capital Group, which staked Valentine, allowing him to form a $3 million venture fund in 1974. #5373. The Key Numbers I’m Watching As Anthropic Makes Its IPO Debut

Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The company says revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero.

The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing.

Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments.

I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns.

OpenAI’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users.

By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1, the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record.

Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it says it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology.

Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets:

Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn-led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion.

Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google, Amazon, Spark Capital, Menlo Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow.

The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension.

The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services.

That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses.

Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption.

Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company says it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. Anthropic points to its launch of Mythos as an example of that balance.

As Anthropic debuts tomorrow, I’ll be watching how well it balances AI’s promise with the risks its own filing lays out.

#5372. GTA 6 Flu Is Here: The Impact on Crypto Markets

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

GTA 6 has finally arrived, and millions of gamers are putting everything else on hold, including crypto portfolios.

After 13 years of waiting, Rockstar’s blockbuster release is already disrupting workplaces, dominating social media, and pulling gamers away from their usual routines. Even our newsroom is feeling the impact, with maybe 30% of employees taking days off.

Tonight, the HEAT trade Miami for Vice City when they host the Milwaukee Bucks on a never-before-seen court, wearing an all-new uniform.Tune in to the NBA on ESPN at 7PM ET for A Night in Vice City.Find out how to watch in your area at https://t.co/sLWQH9hxi7 pic.twitter.com/zeihbzB7th

Could GTA 6 be stealing retail’s attention just as digital asset markets struggle to bring individual investors back?

The scale of the launch is hard to ignore. GTA 6 sold around 17.1 million copies before its worldwide release. The game also carries expectations of $1.85 billion in revenue during its first three days.

Workers are making room for it, too. UKG data covering two million US employees showed time-off requests for launch day running about 20% above normal levels. A separate Zety survey found 22% of Gen Z workers planned around the release.

That is a sizeable chunk of the demographic that crypto platforms have spent years trying to attract. The overlap of both gaming and crypto competes for online attention, particularly among younger audiences who spend hours on streaming platforms, social media and digital communities.

For us, checking Bitcoin prices, chasing the latest meme coin and following market-moving posts can easily become part of the daily routine. But GTA 6 offers something considerably more entertaining than watching another sideways trading session.

The launch is also driving enormous engagement across YouTube and Reddit. Sensor Tower estimates point to more than 50 million additional visits to food delivery and restaurant apps in the US over 30 days.

Crypto’s social media ecosystem could find itself competing for a much smaller share of that attention.

There is another reason the timing is interesting. Retail crypto trading has been weakening even as the broader market has attracted fresh capital.

Data reported from eToro clients placed 62% fewer crypto trades in October than a year earlier. Robinhood’s crypto trading volume also fell 48% year over year in the third quarter, while Coinbase consumer spot volume dropped 59%.

The figures show that rising market valuations have not translated into the same level of retail trading activity seen during previous cycles.

This leaves crypto exposed to competition for speculative attention. Institutional investors can continue trading through market cycles, but retail often depends on excitement, momentum, and whatever narrative is dominating the internet.

But GTA 6 has all three. The game could temporarily pull casual traders away from exchanges, particularly those who spend their evenings chasing small-cap tokens and following crypto KOLs. Meme coins could be especially vulnerable if their usual audience spends the next several days exploring Vice City instead.

There is also an ironic possibility that GTA 6 could create fresh opportunities for crypto speculation. Gaming-themed tokens and GTA-related meme coins could attract traders looking to profit from the launch itself.

Bitcoin does not need gamers watching charts every minute to keep trading. But an industry built around speculation, online communities, and retail enthusiasm cannot afford to ignore where that attention goes.

#5371. Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

#5370. October 28, 2019

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it announced two years ago.

Rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is currently hosting a summit where Case announced the new fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

Very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

Certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

#5369. Anthropic Closes Up 17% After Massive IPO

Shares of Anthropic closed up 17% in first-day trading Thursday amid an otherwise down day for the broader market.

Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday evening, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing.

The offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, including 23.6 million from selling shareholders, up from it’s earlier plan to sell just over 800 million shares. At that upgraded size, the offering is bringing in around $80 billion for the company.

Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

Put together, the IPO and private placement total around $106 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX, by comparison, raised $86 billion in its June offering.

The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books.

For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago.

Anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.
