#5368. So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

“It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.”

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5367. XRP Ledger Activity Hits New November Highs as Batch, Ticket Usage Surge

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Data from XRPL explorer Bithomp reveals that the Batch and Ticket features on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) are increasingly being adopted, with both setting new daily records in November.

The data indicates an increasing use of two XRPL features intended to enhance transaction flexibility and efficiency on the network.

Batch activity reached a new daily high for the month at 1.962 million on November 3, 2026. Ticket activity came next at 1.553 million on November 7, 2026, also setting a new November record. The increase indicates that these features are being embraced in the XRPL ecosystem. Batch functionality allows multiple transactions to be grouped and executed together and was activated on the XRPL mainnet on October 9, 2026.

The growth in batch activity, which neared 2 million on November 3, 2026, comes less than one month after its launch.

This is significant, as Batch is a prerequisite or accelerant for several high-value XRPL use cases already under contract or in the active pipeline, including atomic multi-party settlements. Institutional workflows (custody transfers, DvP settlement, cross-border payment finalization) require two or more accounts to act simultaneously.

On the other hand, tickets provide a way to reserve transaction sequence numbers, giving users more flexibility in managing transactions.

XRP Ledger metrics are in the green, with the transaction count up 75.9% to 4.3 million; active accounts jumped 128%, while XRP burned as fees rose 136%. Payments volume surged 137% in the last 24 hours to $1 billion, according to XRPScan data, while NFT mints rose 240% in the same timeframe.

Not only is the XRP Ledger seeing increased activity, but Ripple led stablecoin market cap growth by issuer over the past 24 hours, up $90.9 million, 4x the next issuer, multipli.fi, at $21.3 million.

Ripple's RLUSD market cap has grown 96% this year, across Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, to $2.7 billion from $1.4 billion in January. Most of that growth came in July, when Ripple launched Ripple Mint. RLUSD market cap stood just under $1.5 billion that month and rose to $2.3 billion by August.

In a milestone for the network, one year ago today, the first US ETF to hold only XRP began trading. Since then, US spot XRP ETFs have accumulated over 1.16 billion XRP.

#5366. October 29, 2019

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he says that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

The now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the company has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as quickly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

#5365. Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Shows Us Why

Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. Trading can swiftly become a barometer of emotions, rather than a well-informed gauge of value.

We have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model. The doom-laden talk of the SaaSpocalypse was noise, with little signal, and most traders were initially unable to distinguish between a company that will thrive in the AI age and one that will be decimated by it.

The SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software. It revealed the limits of public markets in judging its value.

This pattern erodes trust in the public markets. For companies, being publicly owned may no longer be appealing, and founders considering an exit may not view an initial public offering as the ultimate goal.

The markets have struggled to keep up with the tech advances of the AI era and judge their impact on incumbent companies. Sometimes they underreacted and ignored these developments, and other times they overreacted and panicked.

When OpenAI launched ChatGPT to the public in November 2022, Alphabet stock was punished even though later Google emerged as a clear winner with generative AI. And with SaaS, the markets were slow to respond to the advent of generative and agentic AI through to the end of 2025.

The market capitalization of enterprise software companies continued to rise through this period, until January 2026 when all hell broke loose. The launch of Claude Cowork triggered a panic, especially when additional plug-ins were announced later that month that targeted specific workflows for enterprise support functions such as HR and legal.

From there, valuations went into a tailspin, with traders treating software companies indiscriminately. Over two days, an estimated $285 billion of market capitalization was wiped from software, data analytics and financial tech companies, and by April the benchmark cloud software index — the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index —  had dropped by 31% since the start of the year.

As an investor in software over many decades, I have seen this pattern many times before. AI does not mean the end of software companies. Rather, AI has driven a shift in how software is built, where user growth will come from — primarily agents rather than humans — and in the sources of defensible competitive advantage. This was always going to benefit some companies, like those deeply embedded into their customers’ core business processes, and harm others.

There were predictions of the death of SaaS, but this is the hype cycle pattern that always plays out when new technology emerges: a surge of excitement, then a correction, then productivity. In the short term, the markets overestimated the harm AI would inflict on the software sector as a whole.

That is now being corrected as the markets start to realize which companies benefit from AI and which are threatened by it. At the end of October, the cloud software index was up by 26% since the start of the year and by a massive 83% since its nadir in April.

At my firm, Oxx, we never believed in the SaaSpocalypse, and the markets have recovered from this turmoil. The recovery is bifurcated with some sub sectors, like cybersecurity and data and analytics, faring well while others, like workflow management, have fallen back.

In cybersecurity, a great example is CrowdStrike, whose share price dropped by 27% in early 2026 but was up 114% between the start of the year and the end of October.

The knee-jerk reactions to the latest developments with AI, however, are not just temporary market sentiment. They are part of a broader shift that has occurred since the late 1990s and accelerated in 2002 when the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to improve investor protections in the wake of the dot com crash.

It produced the unintended consequence of driving company ownership from public to private markets. While the number of public companies in the U.S. has halved, private markets have grown dramatically in recent years. This is where much of the smart money can be found, along with a more accurate, and patient, assessment of software companies’ value.

The panic over the SaaSpocalypse has shown that the public markets aren’t an accurate reflection of the intrinsic value of many software companies. This disconnect may be causing a systematic mispricing of private company transactions — multiple transactions which had been in process early this year fell away in the wake of the false signals which came from public markets. This needs to be addressed. At the moment, few people recognize there’s a problem with the pricing function of public markets, and the first step to solving this issue is to recognize there is actually a problem.

Richard Anton is the co-founder and general partner of Oxx, a specialist software investor backing European founders on a mission to transform their industries with AI at the moment they’re readying to scale.

#5364. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

#5362. October 31, 2019

Album VC, a Lehi, Utah-based early-stage venture firm that’s been known until now as Peak Ventures, just gathered up $75 million in capital commitments for its third early-stage fund.

The development shows investor confidence in Album’s young team, which came together in 2014 after the founder of Zinch — a site connecting colleges and students that sold to the ed-tech company Chegg in 2011 — decided to try his hand at investing in other startups.

As that founder, Sid Krommenhoek — who stayed on with Chegg for several years, running its international efforts — explains it, “I thought I’d do another startup. But I also knew from our own experience in struggling to raise money the need for more capital in Utah, and I thought having that operator-entrepreneur perspective could be useful.”

A first fund, like many in the industry, was more of an experiment, though it was a decent $23 million, thanks largely to the support of Chegg CEO Dan Rosensweig, who was early to commit capital to the fund. A second ($56 million) fund followed when Krommenhoek and John Mayfield — a friend who joined him from a marketing role at Qualtrics — began investing more seriously in their backyard and beyond.

They were soon joined by a third investor, Diogo Myrrha, who began as a principal with the firm and is now a general partner. Explains Krommenhoek of one of the many things that binds the three Brigham Young University grads, “We all came into Utah’s orbit when it wasn’t necessarily a place where you could live out your career, but that’s changed.”

Bitwise’s Hunter Horsley has shared a glimpse into what might define the cryptocurrency market in 2027.

In a post on X, Horsley reflected on the institutional shift that happened in 2026, writing, "The story of 2026 will have been that the financial institutions all joined team crypto." Horsley also mentioned a recent X post by Charles Schwab, which said that crypto is playing an increasing role in many Americans’ investment journeys, citing the 2026 Modern Wealth Survey.

Charles Schwab everyone The story of 2026 will have been that the financial institutions all joined team crypto. 2027…

The Modern Wealth Survey is an online study conducted for Charles Schwab by Logica Research among a national sample of Americans from August 24 to September 17, 2026.

Charles Schwab’s survey results show that cryptocurrency investors are planning to invest more in the coming months, which will boost adoption. More than half of all respondents (60%) expect to add to their holdings in the next 12 months, compared with ETF owners (56%) and stock owners (52%).

The interest of the participants is driven by the long-term potential. Growth potential and portfolio diversification are the most commonly cited benefits by owners and those interested in crypto. According to the survey, more than half of Americans familiar with cryptocurrency say it is important or essential to building wealth.

Half of those who own cryptocurrency see it as a complement to traditional investments, while more than two in five Americans familiar with cryptocurrency expect it to become a more popular investment; Millennials are the most likely generation to own and be interested in cryptocurrency.

In the EY-Parthenon and Coinbase 2026 survey, 73% of institutions intend to increase their digital asset investments this year. AIMA and PwC find 55% of traditional hedge funds now hold crypto, up from 47% in 2024.

But that demand flows mostly into passive wrappers. Of those surveyed, 81% prefer spot exposure through a registered vehicle. This is seen as a reflection of market infrastructure rather than manager selection.

#5360. RBC Signals brings in $10M investment to expand strategic frontiers for satellite services

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

#5359. What’s Next For Recruiting, Job Hunting And HR? More AI, Of Course

AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

By far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor says it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

Agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

#5356. The Blue Economy: The World’s Quietest Economic Engine And Its Smartest Cities

The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy.

For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources.

The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central.

Powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea.

Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge.

Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end.

The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end.

The drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026).

Blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups.

We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density).

The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies.

The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy?

Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy.

And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook.

To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation.

While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy.

The result is a picture that shows the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy.

To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units.

Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges.

Early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona, a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge.

Notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them.

Get the full story in Mind The Bridge’s report, available for free download here.

Alberto Onetti is chairman of Mind the Bridge and a professor at University of Insubria. He is a serial entrepreneur who has started three startups in his career, the last of which is Funambol, among the five Italian scaleups that have raised the largest amount of capital. He is recognized among the leading international experts in open innovation and has wide experience in setting up and managing open innovation projects — venture clients, venture builders, intrapreneurship, CVCs — with large multinational companies, as well as advising and training on this subject. Onetti has a column on Sifted (Financial Times) and several other tech blogs.

#5354. With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips

Fractile, a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated.

Alongside the likes of Axelera, Etched, and OLIX, this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production.

However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips.

As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source.

Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot, its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual trade-off between memory and capacity.

This trade-off has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date.

In a LinkedIn post, Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.”

Veteran trader Peter Brandt has posted an alarming warning about Bitcoin (BTC), suggesting that the world's largest cryptocurrency might never return to its previous all-time high.

In a recent post on X, Brandt shared a weekly Bitcoin chart showing what appears to be a massive head-and-shoulders formation, a technical pattern commonly associated with a bearish trend reversal.

The legendary trader's warning comes amid one of Bitcoin's worst sell-offs this year, with the cryptocurrency losing nearly half of its value since reaching its record high in October 2025.

Brandt's chart shows Bitcoin forming a left shoulder, a higher peak representing the head, and a lower right shoulder. The cryptocurrency is now testing the neckline of this potential bearish formation, located around the $60,000 to $65,000 region.

Is this a legit H&S top in Bitcoin? If it is I can build a technical narrative that the ATH is in, not to be surpassed at least in my lifetime https://t.co/yoBq2Gp9UK

A confirmed breakdown below the neckline could indicate that Bitcoin has entered a prolonged bearish trend.

However, Brandt has not declared the pattern complete. His warning remains conditional on whether the formation proves to be a legitimate head-and-shoulders top.

Bitcoin suffered another massive crash on Saturday, Nov. 14, extending the losses that had already shaken the cryptocurrency market earlier in the week. The flagship cryptocurrency plunged to approximately $62,830, with its weekly losses exceeding 16%.

The downturn accelerated on Nov. 13, when Bitcoin fell below the psychologically important $70,000 level for the first time since August.

The selloff was initially triggered by worsening macroeconomic conditions, particularly stronger-than-expected U.S. inflation data that increased expectations of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December.

A stronger U.S. dollar and rising Treasury yields and the Nvidia chaos have also made riskier assets, including cryptocurrencies, less attractive to investors.

On Nov. 10, 2021, Bitcoin reached what was then a historic high of approximately $69,000.

Five years later, the cryptocurrency has fallen below that level.

For comparison, Bitcoin closed at approximately $65,467 on Nov. 14, 2021. At the $62,830 level shown on Brandt's chart, Bitcoin was trading roughly 4% below its price exactly five years earlier.

Bitcoin's most recent all-time high was recorded on Oct. 6, 2025, when the cryptocurrency surged above $126,000.

That historic rally was supported by strong institutional demand, substantial inflows into U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, and the increasingly crypto-friendly regulatory scene.

#5352. Stablecoin Market Loses Billions: Where Is Crypto’s Liquidity Going?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Crypto’s stablecoin market has shed $16 billion in a month, marking its sharpest contraction since the 2022 bear market. The retreat is hitting USDT and USDC hard, leaving fewer dollar-backed tokens circulating.

Total stablecoin market cap is now standing at $283 billion, plunges by more than 5% in just a month, losing $16.5 billion in just a month. The decline puts the market under pressure just as crypto struggles to recover, with investors showing little appetite for buying the dip.

Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC account for most of the latest contraction. USDT is holding a market cap of $175.02 billion, down 4.3% over 30 days, while USDC fell to $68.58 billion, losing 5% during the same period. Together, the two stablecoins represent 86% of the entire market.

The contraction also extends beyond dollar-backed tokens. Sky Dollar’s USDS supply dropped 22.32% over 30 days, while Ethena’s USDe expanded 4.36%. The gap shows that some are still moving between stablecoin products.

The pressure is also visible in exchange reserves. A November 11 CryptoQuant’s data showing USDT market cap had fallen $6.6 billion over 60 days through November 7. It was more than twice the $3.2 billion decline recorded after FTX collapsed in December 2022.

The current contraction brings back an ugly history. Stablecoin supply reached $161.5 billion in March 2022 before entering a prolonged decline. Terra’s UST collapse accelerated the withdrawal of capital, with nearly $30 billion disappearing from stablecoin supply in June alone.

That monthly decline was almost twice the latest $16.5 billion contraction this time. Back in 2022, the damage continued into the following year. By September 2023, aggregate stablecoin supply had fallen by 26% from its March 2022 peak, a contraction of $43 billion.

Bitcoin endured a similar period of weakness. After reaching nearly $69,000 in November 2021, BTC eventually plunged to around $15,500 in November 2022. Stablecoin supply continued shrinking even after the initial market shock initiated by Terra. Crypto’s liquidity problems then became a prolonged market condition.

Yet, in 2023, not every stablecoin experienced the same fate. We had a $13.3 billion increase in USDT supply from its November 2022 lows, while USDC lost $16.7 billion. During that period, investors were not simply abandoning every stablecoin. Some were moving toward Tether as the market reassessed issuers and available returns.

This time, arguably, the stablecoin contraction is happening against a different market backdrop. Crypto traders have fewer reasons to keep large amounts of capital parked in stablecoins when Bitcoin and major altcoins struggle to attract buyers. Some holders may be redeeming their tokens for traditional dollars, while others are moving into interest-bearing assets outside crypto.

A shrinking stablecoin market does not mean every dollar has left digital assets. But the simultaneous decline in USDT and USDC supply makes the latest contraction harder to dismiss as simple rotation between issuers.

A crypto recovery needs buyers willing to commit fresh capital, and stablecoins have historically provided traders with an immediate way to enter the market.

#5351. Nine Korean startups vie for a spot in Disrupt 2027’s Startup Battlefield 200 competition

TechCrunch’s yearly Startup Battlefield 200 competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference.

This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at DETO 2026, a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200.

The startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine startups are looking to enter the U.S. market as part of the broader international expansion plans.

Voinosis, which develops AI to detect changes in brain health through voice analysis, won the competition. The other eight startups are listed below in alphabetical order.

Voinosis is developing an AI tool that analyzes speech patterns such as pitch, pauses, rhythm, and response times to detect changes linked to brain health. Each voice check takes less than five minutes.

The company says its technology has been tested in Greek, Japanese, and English, and its product doesn’t require separate training for each language. In a clinical study involving 146 participants, the startup claims its tech achieved 88% accuracy in screening for potential cognitive issues.

Voinosis targets hospitals, senior living facilities, insurers, and individual consumers. It also plans to link voice checks with cognitive training, assessments, and treatment provided by healthcare professionals.

The startup was founded by Grace Shin, who spent more than 25 years as an otologic surgeon. The startup is currently raising a Series A round and has already secured a South Korean pharmaceutical company as a strategic investor.

Awesome Lab, based in Seoul, makes ThermoFlux, a heating system that uses water electrolysis and ionization to generate heat. The system can manage heat production for buildings, water supply, and industrial processes. The company says its technology can reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions.

For its international expansion, Awesome Lab is taking a different approach in each market. In the U.S., it plans to supply core OEM modules and work with boiler, water heater, and HVAC companies on product development.

Crosshub helps travelers and international visitors verify their identities and set up payment methods abroad. Its platform, IDBlock, combines identity verification and payment services using self-sovereign identity (SSI) and zero-knowledge proof.

The company says its platform helps users prove their identity across borders without sharing unnecessary personal information. Crosshub is also integrating this technology with payment systems to improve access to financial services for travelers.

DeepFusion AI has developed a 4D radar-based imaging system with additional sensors for autonomous mobility, robotaxi, maritime surveillance, and defense applications. The system combines RF sensors with radar and lidar to detect objects, movement, or distance without a direct line of sight. All sensors are supposedly packed into a single, customizable unit.

EFLOW develops special motors that can produce more torque, or rotational force, while taking up less space for use in robots, drones, satellites, and other mobility applications. The startup also develops actuators that control how robotic joints move.

Otiton Medical makes two medical devices: One specializes in measuring body temperature, while another can capture ear canal images and analyze the eardrum. The company says its AI was trained on about 55,000 images of eardrums, and the device has received medical certification in South Korea.

Riibotics says it can deploy robots into warehouses within a day. Riibotics wants to reduce deployment costs for warehouses by streamlining setup, which includes infrastructure setup, warehouse mapping, system integration through custom middleware, task programming, and safety checks.

Ternell, a semiconductor startup based in Ulsan, is developing a new type of memory to help AI chips use less power.

Unlike conventional two-state memory, Ternell’s T-SRAM system adds a third state for more efficient data storage. Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips showed a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional SRAM.

Testbank is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions.

The startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. Solve lets you write answers directly on the page and be graded automatically.

#5350. Tom Lee Reveals Three Possible Reasons Behind Crypto Market Crash

Prominent market analyst and BitMine Immersion Technologies chairman Tom Lee has offered three potential explanations for the recent crypto market crash that has erased billions in market capitalization over the last few days.

Firstly, Lee points out that the recent crash in AI and semiconductor stocks, especially Nvidia, may have led to margin calls, particularly for retail investors in Asian markets.

According to the analyst, this scenario might have forced investors who needed more liquidity to cover their leveraged positions to sell other assets, including crypto.

Secondly, Lee explains that investors may be selling off their existing equity and crypto holdings to free up funds ahead of Anthropic’s upcoming IPO.

Lastly, the aftermath of the huge $6.3 billion Binance hack that occurred in late October may also be playing a role.

According to Lee, some account holders may be cashing out or converting their recovered funds into stablecoins, further contributing to the sell-off.

Aside from that, Lee has also cited potential risks posed by AI to existing cybersecurity systems and increased U.S. scrutiny of semiconductor sales to Asian markets, including China, as additional factors.

However, these are all just potential explanations rather than confirmed reasons for the downturn.

On Friday, Nov. 13, the world’s largest crypto asset, Bitcoin, fell below the psychological level of $70,000.

Further selling occurred on Saturday as BTC dropped below $66,000 and continued to decline to around $62,112 as of Sunday, its lowest level since July.

As for Ethereum, the losses are even worse, with ETH dropping to around $1,711, its lowest price since early July.

Major crypto assets like XRP and Solana (SOL) are also experiencing massive losses.

With such a sharp decline, there’s been another round of liquidations in the crypto market.

According to CoinGlass data, about $2 billion in leveraged crypto positions have been liquidated in the last 24 hours, with the majority involving bullish traders.

Additionally, this crypto crash has coincided with massive outflows from crypto exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

From Oct. 30 to Nov. 13, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw nearly $3 billion in net outflows, indicating that institutional investors are also selling off.

#5347. Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots

A new iOS app called Phota Labs gives users access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image.

Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos.

The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop.

The duo saw a gap in the editing tools on the market and believed that although editing tools can be powerful for enhancing photos, they aren’t very effective at fixing a photo that wasn’t captured well in the first place. Phota Labs changes that by focusing on fixing the shot itself while preserving the natural appearances of those in the image.

“Phota is your personal photo assistant that can make great photos for any moment you want to keep before you even ask, which means that it’s a very proactive experience,” Zhang told TechCrunch in an interview. “Think of it almost like a photographer or virtual photographer who looks over your camera roll and tries to understand what’s happening and how they could have taken that photo for you on the spot for that scene.”

The idea is to use AI to transform photos, whether that’s turning a wide-angle group photo into a tighter portrait or transforming a selfie into a regular shot.

Users can choose from different photography styles that determine how AI transforms their images, ranging from subtle edits that preserve the original lens and composition to more dramatic transformations that introduce effects like fish-eye lenses, alternative angles, and entirely different perspectives.

While some people turn to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools to enhance or edit images, these tools can often alter a person’s appearance, especially when working with blurry photos because they don’t know what that person actually looks like.

“For Phota, we built our own tech,” Zhang said. ”We built this personalization technology that actually learns about people’s identity and is able to preserve them in any transformation we do to a photo.”

Images edited with Phota Labs feature invisible watermarks that identify them as altered by AI when shared on social platforms.

The startup is initially targeting people who take tons of photos and like to share them on social media, but don’t want to deal with the tedious process of editing photos. Over time, the founders envision a broader audience, from retirees looking to create beautiful photos for their grandchildren to parents who want to share polished family albums with friends and relatives.

“We have this obsession with authenticity,” Xia said. “I think there’s so much value in connecting AI with real moments and making sure those photos are not perfect, in a sense. That’s why we spend a lot of research into understanding personal context, into building this identity model because we want to make sure the photos are authentic. They’re just better photos of the same moment, rather than saying, ‘Oh, this is an AI image’.”

Xia said beta users were excited to see better versions of moments they had actually lived and saw the results as photos of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders discovered that users were taking more photos because they knew Phota Labs could enhance them later.

“We’re turning something that’s unusable into something that people want to print,” Zhang said. “People who just love photos but never really got into editing can now experience professional quality that could never have been possible. So, I think that meant so much to us. There’s so many cherished moments for photos, and we really want them to be actually meaningful and something that you can remember.”

In terms of funding, the company raised a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year.

Phota Labs is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model. The startup also plans to launch an Android app in the future.

#5346. Binance Pays Microsoft and Applied Materials Dividends on Tokenized Stocks: How Much Holders Get

Binance said on Monday, November 16, that it will pass the next Microsoft and Applied Materials cash dividends to holders of its tokenized stocks, MSFTB and AMATB. It will snapshot balances on Thursday, November 19, the same day both stocks go ex-dividend.

Tokenized stocks are crypto tokens that track a real share, held by a custodian, and trade around the clock. Binance’s versions, called bStocks, do not pay the dividend in cash. Instead, the net amount is reinvested, and each holder’s token balance grows slightly.

We compared both tokens with the real shares since late August. During market hours, they tracked closely. Over weekends, their price called Monday’s opening move only half the time.

Here is what holders get, and what the token prices tell traders this week.

Both companies declared their payouts in September. Microsoft will pay $0.98 a share, up from $0.91. Applied Materials, a maker of chipmaking equipment, will pay $0.53 a share. Both go to shareholders of record on November 19 and are paid on December 10.

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

Binance does not state the tax rate. The standard U.S. rate on dividends paid to foreign holders without a tax treaty is 30%. At that rate, we worked out what holders get:

A dividend only matters if the token tracks the stock. So we compared both tokens with the real shares, using Binance hourly candles and Nasdaq prices since late August.

During market hours, the match is close. At the Nasdaq close, the tokens sat at a median 0.06% from the official closing price across 58 sessions. The widest gap was 0.28%.

Weekends are different. The tokens keep trading while Wall Street is shut, so we checked whether their weekend price predicted Monday’s opening move.

Thin trading in tokenized stocks explains part of it. MSFTB traded about $183,000 in the past 24 hours on Binance, and AMATB about $114,000. This weekend, AMATB stood 1.8% below Friday’s $370.50 close on Sunday night, while MSFTB was down 0.2%. On our numbers, those weekend quotes said little about where the stocks would open.

On the 4-hour chart, where each candle covers four hours, MSFTB trades at $527.61 on Binance. It sits just above its 50-period exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $526.02, and its 200-period EMA at $526.95. With both averages flat and close together, the trend is neutral.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

For holders of tokenized stocks, the dividend adds about a tenth of a percent to their balance this quarter. The bigger lesson is in timing: on weekdays, the tokens follow the stock, but weekend prices are a weak guide to Monday.

#5345. Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands

Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.

Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular.

Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”

Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals.

Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers.

The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents.

This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.

#5344. New Monero Privacy Update Might Be Coming Soon: Key Improvement

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Monero contributor has opened a pull request that changes how nodes relay transactions coming from Tor and I2P, according to the project's GitHub.

PR 11743 was opened on November 13 and is currently pending review. It is an updated version of a PR opened on November 8 by contributor vtnerd. After receiving feedback from another Monero developer, vtnerd, the PR was updated.

The issue lies in a mechanism where a node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P and then passes it to the regular Monero network.

Currently, when a Monero node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P, it relays that transaction to the rest of the Monero network.

While the transaction is technically private as it travels into the node, once it reaches Monero's public peers, the transaction is no longer private. This PR proposes that Monero nodes will only accept transactions from Tor and I2P peers over incoming connections. Transactions received over outgoing Tor and I2P connections would be ignored.

Once accepted, the transaction would be subject to a random delay before being relayed to the rest of the Monero network using Monero's existing transaction relay protocol, Dandelion++. Currently, a user can instruct their node to broadcast their transaction immediately.

Over Tor and I2P connections, this request would be ignored. No transaction would be exempt from the random delay.Being able to link a transaction's timing between the anonymity network and the Monero network is an easy way to deanonymize a user. If a transaction is broadcast to the Monero network immediately after being received from Tor, an observer watching both networks can link the two.

This is a similar concept to a previous PR from vtnerd that would have introduced a randomized delay when relaying transactions from Tor and I2P to the Monero network.

While the amount of code that would need to be modified is not particularly large, this does close a hole for users that rely on Tor and I2P to obscure their location.

When the patch lands in a release is yet to be confirmed. The PR is also labeled for a backport, so it might reach the current release branch as well.

#5343. AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

The price of XRP fell to $0.89 overnight on Nov. 15, and the cryptocurrency hit its lowest level in two years, according to TradingView. XRP first dropped below $1 on Nov. 13 for the first time since mid-August, and the decline continued over the weekend. At press time, XRP has recovered to $0.963.

At the moment the price of XRP reached $0.89, Whale Alert flagged two transfers of 120 million XRP each, worth a combined $215.2 million. The transfers were made seven minutes apart, according to XRPSCAN and Bithomp data.

Both transfers went through the same three wallets, XRPSCAN data shows. The coins left an unlabeled address starting with rGMiNv, went to an intermediate wallet starting with r3bh7p and then moved almost instantly to a third address starting with rpxh7h. After the second transfer, only 98 XRP remained on the first address.

TrackWhale marked the activity of these wallets as "~ Rotation". None of the three addresses is linked to a crypto exchange or to Ripple's escrow accounts, according to XRPSCAN, and the owner of the wallets is not known.

The 240 million XRP did not reach any exchange after the transfers, according to XRPSCAN data.

The drop in XRP comes amid outflows from U.S. spot XRP ETFs. According to SoSoValue, the funds recorded net outflows of $19.13 million between Nov. 9 and Nov. 13, and it was their worst week since March 2026.

Besides, Glassnode data shows that the combined market cap of the USDT and USDC stablecoins went down by $17 billion over the past month to $244 billion.

After Bitcoin fell below $67,000, XRP futures liquidations reached $27 million in 24 hours, and 97% of them were long positions, according to CoinGlass. Loans backed by cbXRP were also liquidated on Morpho, according to the DeFi protocol's data.

#5341. Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say

It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.

“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”

Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.

For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”

It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)

Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.

Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.

Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

Shiba Inu (SHIB) has printed a death cross for the first time in 14 months on its daily chart. The 50 MA is below the 200 MA. This death cross follows the last signal, which was back in September 2025.

The latest death cross signal coincides with a sharp price drop, with Shiba Inu falling to unusually low levels below $0.000004.

Cryptocurrencies tumbled over the weekend, with Shiba Inu dropping sharply to a low of $0.0000037 on Saturday, marking four straight days of declines since November 11.

A death cross was completed on its daily chart, reflecting the ongoing selling pressure in the market. Crypto has been pummeled in recent weeks by a confluence of factors; liquidations accelerated over the last 24 hours, reaching a total of $1.96 billion across the market, according to CoinGlass data.

Unlike the abrupt crashes that have punctuated previous crypto downturns, much of the preceding decline unfolded during relatively subdued trading before liquidations accelerated in recent days.

The latest selloff is testing the resolve of some of the cryptocurrency market’s most committed investors, as a succession of setbacks pushes prices toward their lowest levels of the year and major sources of demand weaken.

Stablecoin supply is shrinking fast, dropping $17 billion over the last month, the steepest drop since 2022. As holders swap stablecoins for fiat, they drain buying power from BTC and crypto, analysts at Glassnode said.

It remains to be seen whether buying power returns to the market. According to Bitwise CEO Matt Hougan, "There will be a big buying opportunity at some point, but it's hard to say when."

Shiba Inu rebounded from a low of $0.0000037 on Sunday, but the meme coin remains down 6.87% over the last 24 hours and down 14% over the week.

Further recovery will occur if dip buying gains traction, with the daily 50 MA and 200 MA at $0.000005 marking resistance levels for SHIB's price. Support is expected at $0.000003 if the declines continue.

#5339. Strategy Slows Its Bitcoin Buying as MSTR Stock Slides: Why Has Saylor Eased Off?
